title: Cheap Drones, Dry Taps: The Iran War Opens a New Era of Water Infrastructure Risk
gist: Iran has made water and power infrastructure — especially Gulf desalination plants — a primary deterrence and coercion lever against the U.S. and its allies, repeatedly striking Kuwaiti, Bahraini, and Qatari facilities since Operation Epic Fury began, and thin U.S./allied air-defense interceptor stocks mean a sustained multi-day campaign could trigger water crises within days.

insights.claim: Iranian Foreign Minister Aragchi warned Gulf states that if the U.S. military renewed large-scale strikes on Iran, their critical infrastructure would be struck in response, and Iran's operational history over the following six months confirmed the threat was credible.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Gulf water/power infrastructure is now an explicit, actively-used deterrence lever against U.S. escalation — investors in Gulf utilities, desalination operators, and regional insurers should price recurring attack risk, not a one-off event.
insights.quote: Iranian Foreign Minister Aragchi recently made it clear to Gulf states that if the U.S. military renewed large-scale strikes on Iran, their critical infrastructure would be struck.
insights.locator: Water and energy infrastructure have become one of Iran's main levers

insights.claim: Kuwait first reported damage near a desalination plant early in Operation Epic Fury when debris from an intercepted drone struck the Doha West facility; Iran subsequently struck a Bahraini desalination facility, killed an Indian national at a Kuwaiti power/desalination plant on March 29, and hit an unnamed Kuwaiti desalination plant on April 3.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: A documented pattern of repeated strikes on named facilities (Doha West, Qeshm Island, Bahrain, Kuwait) gives investors a concrete target list for monitoring insurance, outage, and rebuild-capex exposure at Gulf utilities.
insights.locator: Kuwait first reported damage near a desalination plant

insights.claim: As the ceasefire deteriorated into a 'peace-fire,' Iranian strikes hit a Kuwaiti desalination plant on consecutive nights of July 17 and 18, U.S. strikes hit an Iranian electricity and desalination facility in Hormozgan province, and by July 21 Kuwait's electricity ministry reported Iranian strikes on its power and desalination plants for a fourth consecutive night.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Escalation is accelerating in frequency (four consecutive nights) even under a nominal ceasefire, signaling the risk window is widening rather than closing.
insights.quote: Kuwait's electricity ministry reported Iranian strikes on its power and desalination plants for a fourth consecutive night.
insights.locator: By July 21, Kuwait's electricity ministry reported

insights.claim: Available official and major-news reporting does not indicate Kuwait imposed formal water rationing despite the recent wave of strikes, suggesting air defenses and resilience measures have so far held the line, though it is unclear whether they could withstand a more sustained Iranian campaign such as a daily fire rate of 50 drones plus ballistic and cruise missiles aimed at specific plant complexes.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: The stated stress-test threshold (50 drones/day plus missiles) is a concrete scenario for war-gaming Gulf utility and insurance downside beyond currently observed damage.
insights.locator: This time, air defenses and other resilience measures appear to have held the line

themes.theme: Interceptor shortages as the binding constraint

insights.claim: A recent report estimates U.S. forces globally possess fewer than 1,000 Patriot missiles and approximately 250 THAAD interceptor rounds, a shortage that would also constrain defense of the Gulf states and potentially Israel if Iran launched a sustained assault on water facilities and associated power plants.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Hard global inventory numbers (<1,000 Patriot, ~250 THAAD) quantify a binding supply constraint on U.S./allied air defense — a direct read-through to demand for Raytheon (RTX) Patriot production, Lockheed Martin THAAD, and allied interceptor manufacturing capacity.
insights.quote: A recent report estimates U.S. forces globally possess fewer than 1,000 Patriot missiles and approximately 250 THAAD interceptor rounds.
insights.locator: The shortage of U.S. and allied interceptor reloads

insights.claim: Ukraine offers a cautionary counterexample: now that Ukrainian air defenders have run short of high-end surface-to-air missiles, Russia unleashes waves of ballistic missiles and the nightly toll in people and property is grim, illustrating what happens to Gulf water infrastructure once interceptor stocks are exhausted.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Frames interceptor depletion, not initial strike capability, as the real trigger for catastrophic outcomes — a leading indicator to track (allied SAM inventories) rather than strike counts alone.

insights.claim: The authors call for cheaper, more numerous drone interceptors, and argue this is a gap that Ukrainian defense tech providers could likely fill at scale with injections of Gulf State capital into their manufacturing bases.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Flags a concrete investment thesis: Gulf sovereign capital flowing into Ukrainian counter-drone/interceptor manufacturers as a scalable, cheaper alternative to Patriot/THAAD for this threat set.
insights.quote: Cheaper, more numerous drone interceptors are a must — a gap that Ukrainian defense tech providers could likely fill at scale with injections of Gulf State capital into their manufacturing bases.
insights.locator: Cheaper, more numerous drone interceptors are a must

themes.theme: Why water is a uniquely fast-acting coercive weapon

insights.claim: Water disruption can trigger a major crisis within days, unlike oil/gas or food denial campaigns which can be buffered by financial reserves or take weeks to months to bite, especially if an adversary has mapped the water system and combines kinetic strikes with cyber-attacks — both capabilities Iran credibly possesses.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Establishes water as the fastest-acting economic-warfare lever in the Gulf, meaning market and policy reaction to a desalination strike campaign should be priced faster than for an equivalent energy disruption.
insights.locator: Water is unique as an instrument of coercion

insights.claim: Publicly reported figures suggest Qatar's ready water storage covers less than one week at average demand, while Saudi and Kuwaiti disclosures do not permit a reliable countrywide outage-endurance calculation.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Sub-one-week storage buffer at Qatar quantifies the narrow window before a sustained strike campaign forces rationing, informing time-horizon assumptions for regional business-continuity and sovereign-risk models.
insights.locator: Qatar's ready storage appears consistent with less than one week

insights.claim: A very large reverse osmosis desalination facility can require 100 megawatts or more of power — comparable to a hyperscale data center or a small city — meaning a strike on electrical infrastructure will often disable water production as a secondary effect, and integrated thermal desalination plants likely cannot run on temporary power alone because they depend on steam from the co-located power plant.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Power-water coupling means grid strikes are a de facto water weapon; investors should model desalination and power-generation risk as a single combined exposure, not separately.
insights.quote: a very large reverse osmosis facility can require 100 megawatts or more of power
insights.locator: Physical realities make legal assessments very complex

insights.claim: Restoring a damaged desalination/power complex would require global procurement of turbines, generators, transformers, switchgear, and trained personnel in a marketplace already severely strained by datacenter-related demand and broader electricity system expansions, and rebuilders would have to finish before water storage and substitute supplies are exhausted, likely a matter of days to weeks.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Ties Gulf infrastructure resilience directly to the same constrained global turbine/transformer/switchgear supply chain that AI datacenter buildout is straining — a cross-sector bottleneck relevant to power-equipment makers like GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Hitachi Energy.
insights.locator: Water supply recovery requires repairing the associated power plant

insights.claim: A relatively small number of drones, each costing about $50,000 to $75,000 — roughly the price of a typical new American pickup truck — can shut down a water system supplying hundreds of thousands or even millions of people, from distances of hundreds of kilometers or more.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Quantifies an extreme cost asymmetry ($50-75K drone vs. millions-of-people water denial) that underscores why cheap counter-drone defense, not just expensive interceptors, is the higher-leverage investment.
insights.quote: A relatively small number of drones, each costing about as much as a typical new American pickup truck ($50,000 to $75,000, per the BBC), can shut down a water system supplying hundreds of thousands, or even millions of people.
insights.locator: The difference in today's era of increasingly democratized long-range strike

insights.claim: Abu Dhabi has built the Liwa/Al-Dhafra aquifer storage and recovery system, reportedly able to store 90 days of supply for the city by injecting excess desalinated water into aquifers, and Qatar has completed feasibility and pilot work for a similar system that the authors expect the Iran War will accelerate.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Aquifer storage and recovery (ASR) is a proven 90-day resilience technology likely to see accelerated Gulf capex — a specific infrastructure investment theme to watch across GCC water utilities.
insights.locator: Injecting excess desalinated water into aquifers

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia can reroute desalinated water on both the Gulf and Red Sea coasts through a water pipeline network more than 14,000 km long, though it lacks direct cross-peninsula connectivity, and the authors expect Riyadh to pursue a 'hydrovascular grid' strategy mirroring the East-West Oil Pipeline to build true Gulf-Red Sea water connectivity.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Points to a specific forthcoming Saudi infrastructure megaproject (a water-pipeline analog to the East-West Oil Pipeline) that engineering, construction, and pipe-manufacturing firms should watch for tender activity.
insights.quote: It is also likely that Saudi Arabia will consider a \u201chydrovascular grid\u201d strategy that imitates the East-West Oil Pipeline

insights.claim: Kuwait's secondary groundwater resource is brackish and requires treatment to be fully potable, making that backup water supply itself vulnerable to strikes that meaningfully reduce the country's electricity supply.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Shows Kuwait's fallback water source is not truly independent of grid risk, meaning its effective resilience is weaker than groundwater backup alone would suggest.

insights.claim: Article 54(2) of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions prohibits attacking drinking water installations intended to deny civilians their sustenance value, but the prohibition does not apply when a water system is used solely to sustain enemy armed forces or in direct support of military action, and Article 54 also permits a state to destroy water infrastructure on its own territory under imperative military necessity, as Ukraine did breaching a dam on the Irpin River in 2022 to impede Russian forces near Kyiv.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Because most Gulf desalination plants are integrated with power stations serving mixed civilian/military demand, legal accountability for strikes will remain contested — reducing the likelihood of deterrence via international law alone.

insights.claim: The authors add an eighth resilience step to seven previously proposed in a March 2026 War on the Rocks analysis co-written by one of the authors — hardening, spare-parts stocking, onsite power generation, plant dispersion, interconnected pipelines, expanded storage, and dedicated air defenses — namely widespread civil defense training to bolster societal readiness and buy time for governmental responses.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete eight-point resilience checklist investors can use to score which Gulf utilities/governments are ahead or behind on hardening desalination assets.
insights.locator: A March 2026 War on the Rocks analysis
